newsitem.title: UK: Euro Crude Outlook - Iraq's absence to raise value.
newsitem.headline: Euro Crude Outlook - Iraq's absence to raise value.

text.p: European crude values will be buoyed this week by short-term tightness and further delays in the resumed export of Iraqi sour barrels, traders said.
Iraq's key negotiator in its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations said on Saturday he did not anticipate Baghdad restarting crude flows until August.

The market had been relying on an early to mid-July date for the resumption of exports, after Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed last week predicted quick agreement with the U.N. on an aid distribution plan.
But negotiator Abdul Amir al-Anbari foresaw a much later date.

"End of July, beginning of August we would resume our oil discussions. We'll have to sign contracts and they have to be approved by the oil experts in New York," al-Anbari said at a business forum in Switzerland. "Then, the shipments would start."

The price strength that crept into the market by the end of last week as buyers rushed to assure July supplies would not come under pressure until a firm date for Iraq exports was reached, traders said.
"If the oil starts to flow, short-term bullishness could fade very quickly," said one broker.
"The standard explanation for the activity at the moment is pressure from buyers," said the trader, commenting on trade at firmer numbers on Friday.
"But perhaps it's equally a case of suppliers very ready to accept these values before any price fall."
Under the terms of deal struck in December, Iraq is permitted to sell $2.14 billion worth of oil over 180 days to raise money for food and medicine.

The deal was renewed after the first six-month term ended on June 8, but disputes between Baghdad and the United Nations over delays in signing contracts to buy aid with money earned have delayed the start of the second phase.
"My view is mixed," said one senior trader. "It all depends on the Iraqi barrels. If they don't come, there is still quite a bit of tightness there."
He noted one major North Sea producer on Friday had only 13 July cargoes left of Ekofisk, Oseberg and Statfjord, about half the normal amount at this stage of the monthly cycle.

On Friday values firmed on Atlantic Basin supply tightness and the continuing absence of Iraqi barrels. Traders argued that the end of the OPEC's Vienna meeting brought these bullish fundamentals into sharper focus.

Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil trading division of Bankers Trust International in London, said the OPEC deal to freeze output quotas had not changed anything and he expected a bearish reaction over the next few weeks.
OPEC is pumping some two million barrels per day (bpd) above its self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
Brent numbers held firm through last week and edged up at the end. A July 14-16 loader was rumoured to have moved at July Brent -1 cent on Friday, equivalent to around -14 cents against August.
